header.title: Opera attributa. Liber In Genesin: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Vettius Aquilinus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp337.tmp337.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.

The stretch interleaves the poem with the editor's apparatus; references are out of numerical order as the library holds them, and are translated in that order. Line 22a is damaged at its end ('ins(??)'); the final word could not be read. 'Era' in 32 is a scanning error for 'Eva'. In 64a 'Matum' and in 80b 'matum' are read as 'malum'. In the note on 98, 'Mr. Victor' is taken as Marius Victor (Alethia); the quoted lines are partly garbled ('metis (??)', likely 'mentis' with a lost noun; 'angustos' perhaps for 'augustos'), so that rendering is tentative. 'Prasinus' (73) is a green gemstone, perhaps prase or emerald. Line 47 'Metitur solum mordaces volvere curas' is elliptical; rendered as God judging that man alone would brood over cares.

Lines 89–93 (on the serpent's punishment) are confused and probably corrupt, as the editors' notes indicate; translated as they stand. 'pendit' (85b) taken as 'replies'; 'loquetis' read as 'loquelis' per the note; 'vola' (119) read as 'vota'; 'Deminus' (107) as 'Dominus'; 'reddare' (125) as 'reddaris'. Lines 110b–111a are garbled (no verb for the naming; see note 136). In 125a the main verb is missing; Fabricius' 'deducit' supplied. The genealogy follows the poet's forms: 'Naida' and 'Malechus' (for Irad and Mehujael), 'Matusalamus' (for Methushael), 'Amalech' (for Lamech), 'Aelus' (Jabal), 'Jobalus' (Jubal), 'Tobellus' (Tubal-cain), 'Noema' (Naamah); 'Enochus' in 158 is Seth's son Enos in Genesis.

The edition's line references are out of order and the text is often corrupt. Line 1 ('hoc se poscente rogari') is obscure. It is taken to refer to Enos calling on the Lord. In line 6, 'Enochus' must stand for Enos. In line 8 the subject (Mahalalel) is unclear. Line 12: 'sajunior' is read as 'sed junior' (Martène's note 206). Line 31: the text names 'Sethum', but Noah's son is Shem. Lines 32–33, on smiths beating iron, seem misplaced from the account of Tubalcain. 'Innumerum' is read as 'in numerum', following the note. Line 'Assere quadrato nullis censura fluentis': 'censura' is read as 'cessura', following the note. Line 'Lumina restarent, tete jam libera': 'tete' is read as 'tota'. Line 'Quae, nemore invenio': 'invenio' is read as 'invento'. The lines 'Laxat claustra senex, nova semina terrae / Atque Deum gaudens contra se attollere sanctum' have no main verb for their second half. The text of Chapters VIII–IX seems to be missing after them. The line 'Hereum de mors foret quos ardua cervix' is corrupt and could not be construed; it probably concerns Nimrod. Only 'whose lofty neck' is translated. The place names are garbled: 'Orecha' and 'Archata' are probably Erech and Accad, and 'Aeolia' is unclear. 'Sinnacheros' is probably Shinar, 'Robotham' Rehoboth, 'Calcham' Calah, 'Dasemata' Resen and 'Niniveva' Nineveh. 'Hic Babylon collocat' lacks a metrical subject; it is taken to mean Nimrod. 'Lactat' (line 'Haec inter sanctos') is taken in the sense 'entices'.

The stretch interleaves the editor's footnotes (numbered by the edition's own line count, mostly from Martène) with the verse; they are translated as they stand. Line 275a 'Abram odescit': corrupt; the editor proposes 'ditescit' (prospers), followed here. 'pro(??)crem' (292): illegible in the scan, taken as 'procerem' (head) or 'progenitorem'. 295a 'poscit laetos et grandior astu' is obscure and a foot too long (as the edition notes); the rendering is tentative. 307 'selum' read as 'zelum', 308 'amulum' as 'aemulum'. 316 'loetum' read as 'laetum'. 326/405 'perditat' (spoils) is odd for a fertile flooding; possibly corrupt. 344: the poem's names 'Ariae, Hadachar, Godullagomurus, Amarfalus' are rendered by their biblical equivalents Arioch, Chedorlaomer, Amraphel; 'Hadachar' is unidentified (perhaps a distortion of Tidal) and kept as given. 349: 300 + 2×9 = 318, as in Genesis. 364 'emeritum nutum' is obscure.

Several scanning errors read as intended: Subni(??)usque as Subnixusque; lactum (note 449) as factum; laboral as laborat; vales as vates; maenia as moenia; senus as uncertain. Line ref 405a: fulmine signo read as fulmine signum, following the editor's note 503. Ref 560 ('Euge memor vatis pleno non senus anno') seems corrupt; 'non senus' is unintelligible as printed, and '[no longer barren]' is a conjecture. Ref 464: the text has 'Ab his quinque viris'; the editor proposes 'A bis quinque viris' ('by twice five men'), which would match Scripture's ten. Ref 595 breaks off at 're-' (verb lost); 'force' is a guess. Ref 580 is obscure, and the rendering is approximate. Ref 550 'Ipse' is translated as 'Ipsa' per note 550. Ref 585a 'Azym' is read as 'Azyma' per note 585. Ref 472a has Gomorrah where Genesis has Sodom. The peoples at refs 399–402 are rendered by their usual biblical names (Genaei = Kenites, Genezei = Kenizzites, Chalmonei = Kadmonites, Cheti = Hittites, Fereza = Perizzite, Raffana = Rephaim, Jebosacus = Jebusite, Gergessus = Girgashite).

Line 513–514: 'fratris germine creta' would make Sarah the daughter of Abram's brother; the poet's sense is unclear. Line 615 (Lot's daughters) and 645 are loosely attached syntactically; 645 is taken as referring to Abimelech's dream. Line 665 is corrupt in the edition ('Jamque panes cunctos, insumpserat[omne'); translated following the editor's note (Jam panes cunctos, undamque insumpserat omnem). Line 587 'pomae' read as 'formae' per the note; line 598 read with 'consertus' per the note. Line 606 'nihil jam' is suspect (perhaps 'nuper'); 'nidentem' in 755 read as 'nitentem' (eager). Line 610 'Gargara' taken as Gerar. Line 613 is damaged: 't(??)nqat colum' read as 'teneat solum' ('keep to the soil'); uncertain. In 562 the chapter number XXII is presumably an error for XXIII. Footnotes ascribe the poem to Juvencus, following the edition.

Line 6 (769): text 'paterne edisserit acta' is doubtful; the edition's note suggests 'fraterno edisserit actu'. Line 14: 'Horrea mollit(??)' damaged; translated following the note's reading Hordea (barley). Line 15: one word lost before 'eto'. Line 16: 'Noe minus' taken as 'Nec minus'. Line 26: 'Inausos' unclear; translated as 'Infaustos' per the note. Lines 27-28: 'cave' taken as 'cavae', 'in luce' as 'in lucem'. Line 33: 'sagas' taken as tents/coverings. Line 69: sense of 'praenuncia corda' uncertain. Lines 84-85: 'proditi' read 'prodi', 'vicere' read 'visere'; 'Carras' = Carrhae/Haran. Line 104: the poet calls Laban 'gener' (son-in-law), though in Genesis he is Bethuel's son. Line 122: 'praestes' translated per the note as 'praesens tellus'. Line 124: 'aut' read 'haud' per the note. Line 134: 'vatis in devia' is obscure. Line 172: 'parius' perhaps 'pariter'; the names of Bilhah's sons are not given. Line 188: 'mystea' is unidentified (the Vulgate has poplar, almond and plane). Lines 42-43, 95, 97-98: the notes contain unreadable words.

Line 751a 'alitos' is unclear (perhaps 'auctos'); rendered as 'reared'. Line 761 'Nangus' is evidently corrupt; translated as 'nactus' (having found). Line 771 is corrupt (see editor's note 959); sense supplied. Line 975 is corrupt; translated following the editor's conjecture 'caveam'. 'Galatum' is presumably Galeed/Gilead. 'Correus' stands for Shechem son of Hamor (see note 1015). 'Matorum' read as 'natorum'. Lines 833–834 are misplaced and obscure (per editor's notes 1018/1037) and translated as they stand; 837 'quod defore norat' is uncertain. 'Caderae' is the tower of Eder. 854 'gerboso' read as 'herboso'. 1050 'pulchro' is obscure.

Several readings are taken as evident corrections: 'fam' read as 'jam' (861a), 'd pellere' as 'depellere' (884a), 'ab alio' as 'ab alto' (908), and 'silicum' taken as 'cilicium', 'haircloth' (895a). In 891 'urbi' is unclear; it is translated as if 'ubi' ('when'). In 893 'nulla mentitur fraude necatum' is obscure, and the rendering is tentative. In 910b the sense of 'Nec tamen obtinuit Petafretam mitis amore' is uncertain. In 926 'commissit ergastula legat' seems corrupt; it is rendered as if 'commissa ergastula regat'. In 949a 'quae' is rendered as referring to the baskets. In 980a 'juncto tonante' is obscure. In 981 the stray 'es' at the line end is taken as part of 'cura medendi [est]'. The lines of notes keep their proposed Latin readings untranslated, following the earlier practice.

Verse lines are interleaved with the editor's Latin footnotes, which are translated as they stand. Several scanning errors are read as evident: vales for vates (1029, 1064); vice for viae (1034); chororum for charorum (1098); in fit read as infit (1089); vicium probably victum (1075a). 1058 'futurum' is corrupt; it is translated following the footnote's conjecture 'furti tum'. 1084 'Futurum' is likewise read as 'furatum' (thief). 1068–69 are obscure: as printed, Joseph affirms that 'the seer' cleaves to God; the sense may be that their father does. 1340 'fato' is doubtful (the note suggests 'succo'). 1077 'majori' conflicts with Genesis, where Benjamin, the youngest, gets the larger portion; the footnote calls the line faulty. 1049: 'leve olentia' is probably 'bene olentia', 'sweet-smelling'. 997: the sense is incomplete, and a verse may be lost. Petafras is the father of Asenath (Potiphera), a different person from Petafreta (Potiphar).

1124: 'tua praedia' read as 'sua praedia'. 1135a: stray 'l' is a footnote mark. 1135a–1415: the text gives Manasseh the right hand and calls Ephraim the elder, the reverse of Genesis 48; translated as printed, possibly a corruption. 1145a: 'aero' read as 'aevo'. 1144a–1145a: the object of 'adjudicat' (presumably blessings) is not expressed. 1146: 'solo terrenis' is grammatically awkward and may be corrupt. 1147–1430: the subject of 'dedit' is unexpressed (the mourners).

nodes.text: APPENDIX. WORKS ATTRIBUTED TO JUVENCUS.
CHAPTER I. In the beginning the Lord set in place the heaven and the earth:
for the land was formless and hidden by the flood,
and God in his immensity moved over the vast waters;
while chaos and black darkness dimmed all things,
as he parted these from the starry pole, he spoke:
"Let there be light", and all things shone in a joyful world.
And when God had completed the works of the first day,
he founded the sky, growing white with clouds coming to birth.
The immense Sea received the wandering shores,
sweeping along manifold rivers with powerful currents.
The third day, golden, uncovered the face of the lands.
Soon the land, a name being given it, is called Dry.

On this poem I have spoken in the Prolegomena, no. 16 and following. The first four chapters were published from old editions by Andreas Rivinus under this title: The Genesis of Caecilius Cyprianus, or rather of Q. Septimius Florens Tertullianus. I append Martène's notes, to which I add, or among which I insert, a few of my own.
Verse 1. The editions read creavit [created], a word which the Vulgate version uses, unknown to Juvencus. Martène. — The Itala version [has] fecit [made].

2. In the Vulgate edition we read: But the earth was empty and void. But the ancient Italic version, which Augustine cites, has: But the earth was invisible and unformed. Mart. — Rivinus by conjecture reads Jamque [and now] for Namque [for]. Others in Sabatier read with Augustine.
5. Pamelius reads this verse a little differently, namely in this way: As he ordered these to be parted from the pole, he spoke. Mart. Before Pamelius, Morel and Fabricius had read thus.
Flowering shoots spring up in the windswept fields, and at the same time fruit-bearing branches bend down their arms.
On the fourth day he begets the moon together with the lamp of the sun,
and paints the stars shining with trembling light.
These elements he gave as marks to the world beneath,
to teach that the seasons must change through their various risings.
On the fifth day the flowing rivers receive fish,
and birds hold up their bodies on varied wings.
On the sixth the Father makes the cold snakes slither into coils,
and spreads herds of four-footed beasts over all the fields,
and commanded all things to increase everywhere
with manifold offspring, and to roam and feed over the immense lands.
6. The editions [have] claro et, for which Morel reads clare. Mart. — Fabricius reads Lux fiat, et claro. Junius in Rivinus [reads] Lux fiat. claro nituerunt.
7. Fabr.: Cum Dominus primi. So also Morel.
9. Edit., verentia. Mart. Read verrentia [sweeping]. For so Fabr. [has], verrentia littora, after Morel.
13. Rivinus by his own conjecture puts gramina [grasses] for germina [shoots].
15. Martène notes nothing; but Fabricius has Quarta dies, which fits the metre.
16. Edit., fingit [fashions]. Mart. Pingit [paints] is far better.
19. Edit., At quinta, with die omitted, not so well. Mart. The old editors, to accommodate the metre, wrote: At quinta accipiunt.
20. Pamelius reads this verse thus: And birds hold up their varied wings in the air. Mart. Fabricius agrees with Pamelius, but [has] corpore [with the body] for aere [in the air].
21. Edit., Sexta praegelidos [very cold], Mart.
22. Fabr., Quadrupedumque.
When divine power had established these things [...],
seeing that a ruler would be lacking to the affairs of the world,
he says this: "Let us make man exactly
like our countenance, to reign over the whole world."
And although he could have composed him by a word alone,
yet he himself deigned to shape [him] with his holy right hand,
and breathes into the brute breast from his divine breast.
CHAPTER II. After he saw him formed as if in his own likeness,
he judges [that he would] turn over gnawing cares alone.
At once he floods his eyes with watering sleep,
so that, gently, from a rib pulled out a woman might be formed,
and a mingled substance might strengthen the twin bodies;
and a name is given, which means "of life": Eve.
Therefore children by custom leave their parents,
and cling to their wives, having set up their homes.
On the seventh day God rested at the end of his works,
establishing it as hallowed, for the joys of the age to come.
At once, when the throngs of living creatures were presented in order,
to all, one by one, a name that endures is given
by Adam, with the skilful wisdom granted to him.
Him God deigns to address, and Eve joined [to him]:
"Increase with manifold offspring into times to come,
so that the heavens and the lands may be full of your seed,
and as my heirs, pluck the various fruits
which the groves and fields yield from rich turf."
When he had said this, paradise is furnished as a joyful court,
and looks upon the light of the first sun.
Among these grows a tree with deadly fruit,
producing a joined taste of life and death.
In the midst of the dwelling a river flows in a pure stream,
with which it waters the splendid gardens from its clear waves,
and from its surging spring it divides into four channels.
The Pishon, very rich, surges with gold-bearing waters,
and wears down conspicuous gems in its roaring flood:
to one the name is prasinus [leek-green stone], to the other blazing carbuncle;
and with clear shallows it laps along the land of Havilah.
27. Fabr., Haec memorat: Nostris hominem faciamus ad unguem. Morel thus, but in unguem.
29. Edit., hunc uno. Mart.
31. Edit., in pectore; far better our manuscript, a pectore. Mart. Fabricius had already printed a pectore.
31. Rivinus, following Barth's conjecture, reads effigies formatum cui sua vidit.
36. Edit., mixtu gemino. Mart.
37. Fabr., virae for vitae.
40. Edit., Septima quando Deus. Mart.
41. The editions read this verse thus: Sacrata statuens venturi gaudia saecli. Mart. — Fabricius punctuates Sacrata, statuens.
43. Rivinus conjectures: Virtutem cunctis nomen, quod permanet, indit.
44. Edit., a little differently: Adami a Domino donata prudentia solers. Mart. But Fabricius, concerned for the metre, restored: Adami a Domino data quae prudentia solers.
55. Barth suspects ornos [ash trees] for ortus; Rivinus would prefer hortos [gardens].
56. Fabr., undante.
57. Fabr., Phison.
60. Edit., Evilat. Mart.
64. Rivinus wants Adam for Adamus.
After this the Gihon, gliding past, enriches the Ethiopians.
The third is the Tigris, joined to the pleasant Euphrates,
furrowing Assyria apart with swift stream.
Here Adam was placed as guardian with his faithful wife;
and as a worker he is instructed by such words of the Thunderer:
"Do not fear to pluck together the permitted fruits
which the unshorn grove has produced on leafy branch,
[but be] careful that the guilty apple is not perhaps picked,
which flourishes with a twofold sap for separate functions."
Meanwhile another night held them no less blind,
and no garment had yet covered their newly formed limbs.
CHAPTER III. Among these dwellings and gardens with mellow berries
a foaming serpent, surpassing the animals in cunning sense,
was creeping silently in cold coils;
turning over envious lies in its biting mind,
it tempts the soft heart in the woman's breast:
"Tell me, why should you fear the happy offspring of the apple tree?
Did God not hallow all the fruits that have grown?
But if you are eager to pluck the honeyed food,
a golden world will return from the star-bearing pole."
She refuses, and fears to touch the forbidden branches;
but yet her heart is overcome by its weak sense.
At once, as she bit the mellow [fruit] with snow-white tooth,
a clear sky shone forth, stained by no cloud.
Then the taste, putting allurement into her honeyed throat,
drove her to bring the gift to her unaccustomed husband.
As soon as he took it, the night wiped away, shining
and clear their eyes flashed out, as the world grew bright.
So when each looked upon the naked body,
what they see as shameful they shade with fig leaves.
By chance, as the sun's light was now setting, the Lord's
sound they recognise, and fearful they make for out-of-the-way places.
Then the Lord of heaven addresses the sorrowful Adam:
"Tell me, where are you staying now?" He answered, suppliant, thus:
"O Lord, I tremble with fearful heart at your words,
great one, and naked I am worn out by stiffening fear."
Then the Lord: "Who gave you the guilty fruit?"
"The woman handed it over", he says; "at once [our] eyes

68. Edit., legalis. Mart. Barth conjectures, with Rivinus applauding, ne fors malum for ne forte malum. Malum noxale [guilty apple], i.e. pomum noxale [guilty fruit], as below at verse 97: Who gave you the guilty fruit?
71. Morel [has] vestis nec, Fabricius nec vestis.
72. Edit., nota sacravit. Mart.
78. Edit., nota sacravit. Mart.
79. In our manuscript is read: Ad quis; the editions, E queis. Mart. — Fabr., E quis. Martène in the text printed Adqui for Atqui.
80. Edit., remeabit cardine. In the Vulgate the serpent promises knowledge of good and evil: You will be as gods, knowing good and evil. Mart.
85. Fabr., mellitis faucibus, which the law of the metre certainly requires.
86. Edit., Compulit. Mart. — Rivinus with Cauchius [reads] insuetum for insueto.
90. Edit., Cumque pudenda. Mart. — Perhaps Quaeque pudenda for Quaecumque, as quisque for quisquis, quicumque.
96. Edit., metu frigente. Mart.

98. We do not find in the Vulgate that these things were said to Adam by the woman; but Juvencus could have read them in an older version. Mart. — Here perhaps belongs the sense of verse 80, A golden world will return from the star-bearing pole. Thus the author of the poem understands the words of Genesis, Your eyes will be opened. Marius Victor, Genesis: And so God did not wish it lawful for man to pluck the narrow fruits, lest, the mind's [veil] removed, they should cast their eyes into heaven, and know the best things, and be like gods.
were flooded with shining day, and a clear sky
shone upon us, and the sun, and the stars of heaven."
At once the wrath of God terrifies the troubled Eve,
while the Most High seeks the author of the forbidden deed.
She replies to this: "The persuasions of the serpent's speech
I accepted, deceived by trickery and a coaxing request.
For, weaving his words with viperish poisons,
he told me these were sweet above all fruits."
Forthwith the Almighty condemns the dragon's deeds,
commanding the monster to live hated by all,
soon to creep forth with breast spread out, then to chew the ground
with its bite: with a war that would last for all times
among human senses, and that it itself, gliding
with head cast down, should creep prone behind the legs of men
and [their] heels, while, gliding, it presses close at hand.
The woman, wretchedly deceived by fraud-bearing persuasions,
is commanded to bring forth offspring in harsh peril,
and to endure servitude through devotion to her husband.
"But you, to whom the opinion of your wife
seemed true, who, overcome, yielded to the cruel dragon,
will bewail your wretched toil through long ages.
For in place of the shoot of the wheaten harvest there will spring up for you
the thistle, and the Christ's thorn with its many sharp spines,
so that with weary innards and a sorrowful breast
your anxious sustenance may yield very many sighs,
until, at the setting time of coming death,
you are returned to the lying earth, from which you bear your body."
When this was done, the Lord gives the frightened pair weariness of life,
and drives them, cast out, far from the sacred gardens,
103. Editions, loquentis. Far better in our manuscript, loquelis. Mart.
108. Editions, visere. Mart. — Barth had already restored vivere by conjecture, which also pleased Rivinus.

110. Fabricius with Morel, Pandere; Pamelius, Prendere; Rivinus, from Barth's conjecture, Pascere. Rivinus adds that Prendere is less bad than Mandere. Fabricius' reading Pandere sola, i.e. the earth, is unintelligible. Vulgate: You shall eat earth. Other old [versions]: You shall eat earth, you shall chew, earth shall be your food. From which the reading Mandere is confirmed. Virgil, [Aeneid] 11, verse 668 [sic]: He, vomiting streams of blood, falls, and bites the bloody ground.

111. Editions, labantem. Mart. — Rivinus conjectures ipsum esse serpentem, but thinks the passage corrupt. A little later occurs lubens, with the first [syllable] long. This [syllable] is entirely short if labentem is read.
113. Editions, ut calces. Mart. — Rivinus emended: Serpat, at hunc c[a]l[ce]t, dum bellans cominus instat.
114. Fabr., decepta loquelis. For so the metre is respected.

116. Rivinus punctuates: Servitiumque sui studio, Perferte, mariti: for she does not endure the servitude of her husband, but rather [his] dominion, which makes her a servant, and [she endures] this wrong through devotion to her husband.

121. Proba too in her cento borrowed this verse from Virgil, Eclogue 5, verse 39: The thistle, and the Christ's thorn rises with sharp spines. The author of this poem at times brings forward half-lines from Virgil and others for his own purpose.

123. Rivinus emended sollicitus praestet suspiria victus, or with Fabricius sollicitos praestent suspiria victus. So Martène printed it, but did not observe that other editions read sollicitos praestet suspiria victus.
and sets [them] facing away, and shuts [them] out with a fire between,
in which the Cherubim whirls with very swift heat,
while the hot crest seethes and rolls its flames.
For them the Lord, so that their limbs should not stiffen in sluggish cold,
sewed together skins torn from the bodies of cattle,
covering their naked limbs with warm garments.
CHAP. IV. So when faithful Adam felt that he was now
a husband in wedlock, the name of mother [he gives] to his beloved
wife; she bears two offspring from [his] seed.
At once the father names them with different beginnings:
this one has the name Cain; joined to him, Abel
with much care kept the harmless sheep.
But the other turned the earth with the curved plough.
When these were bringing their gifts to the everlasting Thunderer,
they gave different fruits, as their mind prompted.
For the first offered what had sprung from the fertile clods;
but the other devotes himself to a gentle lamb,
bearing in his hand pure entrails and snowy fat,
and at once the pious offering pleases the Lord as he looks on.
On account of this Cain glowed with chill anger,
whom God, deigning to address him, speaks to in these words:
"Tell me, if you live rightly and discern what is harmful,
can you live pure of a crime you have incurred?
Cease to ruin your brother with deadly intent,
who, subject to you as to a master, will offer his neck."
Yet not broken by these [words], [he leads] his brother out to the fields,
and when he saw him caught on the grass of the wilderness,
gnashing, he crushes the innocent throat with both hands.
The Lord, having watched this deed from high heaven,
131. The ancients, as Marius Victorinus notes, used to use quis for queis and quibus, and so this author more than once. Mart.
133. Fabr. and others write Opperiens, so that the first [syllable] is long.
136. Editions, bino qui gemine (read germine) factus. Mart.
138. Editions, Atque Cain hic nomen habet. Mart. — Perhaps Cainus hic nomen habet.

139. Editions, videntes. But the ancients very often used the letter v for b. Mart. — In some editions videntes stands, wrongly, but in Fabricius and others, clearly, bidentes; with this difference, however, not noticed by Martène: cui junctus Abelus: Innocuas hujus servabat cura bidentes, which was done so that with cura in the nominative the verse should stand.
145. Fabr.: Exta manu sincera gerens, adipemque nivalem. This variant reading escaped Martène, and makes for greater elegance of the verse.
147. Junius preferred rapida or gravida in place of gelida.

149. Vulgate: If you do well, will you not receive? But if ill, will sin not at once be present at the door? The author of the poem [follows] the Itala version: If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned. See Sabatier.
150. Fabr., non in place of num.
152. Fabr., daturus in place of praebebit, which the metre rejects.
153. Fabr., Fratrem deducit ad arva.
154. Editions, deserto. Mart.

155. Editions, franges, and that from conjecture. For the manuscript read fraudans; better our manuscript, frendens. Mart. — Fabricius printed fraudans, which Rivinus approves, from fraus, harm. Pamelius had corrected [it to] frangens.
156. Fabr., celso. Morel, more rightly, coelo.
inquires where on earth Abel is living.
He denies that he had been set as his brother's keeper.
God speaks to him: "Does not the voice of his blood
sound, sent to me, and rise up to the lofty sky?
Know therefore what will remain for you for so great a crime;
for the earth which just now grew wet with your brother's blood,
cursed, will refuse to you, hated one, the seeds entrusted [to it],
and, its plants consumed, will bring forth no fruit,
so that, numbed, knocking your limbs together with much trembling,
you may ever draw sighs as though at a funeral close by."
He, terrified, groans, and asks death of the divine power,
which, however, was not granted by the hostile Thunderer;

while they strip the grain amid the fallow fields,

beside which those of his brothers were falling with bowed neck.
After the youth revealed [this] in calm speech,
it stirred their trembling, fearful hearts to uproar,
as they spoke with terrifying murmur of a king and lord;

with all present whom the line of blood binds together.

and the moon joined with it, with its trembling light,
and with these, ten stars rising up joined together,
and bending their curved necks to him as to a lord.

admitting that he was soon to be worshipped by his alarmed brothers,
at once the young men depart, and for their father's flocks
seek out glad valleys through flowery grass;
sent to them, he goes off and wanders through silent thickets,
informed, as a certain young man pointed them out, of the retreats
which the band of brothers had chosen, having changed pasture;
when they could recognize him from afar by his varied garment,

and puts around himself a black covering of haircloth.

1114. Perhaps, amictus. And the following verse seems to need placing before this one.

with platters, and to delight in the din of a great kitchen.

please her gladly, and her womb is filled with a twin pledge,

thrust out and put forth his hand, which the skilful woman
ties with crimson cloth; soon it is hidden back in the womb,
and with their places changed, the other is at once born,
taking the first place, who had been second by lot.
Since this one had once been set apart by a boundary,

CHAP. XXXIX. The Lord's faithful guardianship kept Joseph,
not allowing him to live subjected to a harsh law.
For the master named before gives everything to the servant,
and not with empty hope; for the gentle Lord from on high
increased more abundantly all that the youth was keeping.
Yet the gentle [youth] did not keep Potiphar by love.
For because his eyes shone in his striking face,
the mistress, badly wounded, begs the slave for intercourse.
But the boy shuns the foul thing, and refuses
to press the consecrated bed with immoderate guilt.
But the woman, lost in vain to forbidden flames,
explores the soft approaches and watches for the right times.
By chance, when she found the house empty and him alone, she presses on,
and, gripping him by the hand, forces him to lie down with her.
He leaps up nimbly and takes the garment off his body,
and slips out between his mistress's two arms.
The woman cries out, and draws strength from the crime,
shouting that the very sweet glory of her chastity had been violated
by a young man trusting in his looks, while, wanton in his youth,
he burns, and strives to climb into his master's bed.
Moreover, she addresses her husband in a sad voice,
and wants the innocent defendant subjected to the punishment she desires.
He, thinking these things true, shuts Joseph in prison,
in which punishment was already confining the king's servants.
The keeper of the prison soon soothes him with a kindly heart,
and, seeing him innocent, entrusts the prison to him to govern.
CHAP. XL. There by chance two, whom the grim tyrant in his lofty hall,
moved by a black will, had shut away,
confined, dreaded punishment in trembling hearts,
and while anxious cares were stealing [sleep from] their eyes,
they saw dreams, messengers of things to come.
When he had observed them, gloomy, with clear-sighted eye,
he asks the causes, and makes them confess the hidden things.
At once the one who served the customary wine to the tyrant
tells what had been seen in the sleepy night:
1131. Perhaps, Nec spes.

as it creeps, and hangs bound from its own lash,

foamed with fresh must, which my right hand pressed,
which my lord took and held in his ready palm.'
Then the youth reveals all the hidden things clearly:
that the three stocks are three days, after which
[the king] restores him to what he lost, and he regains favour,

'that, when you have gained confidence to speak,
you remove my punishment, [incurred] for no crime.

by my brothers' crime, I went, though nobly born, into slavery.'

and his severed head fixed on a tall stake,

CHAP. XLI. Meanwhile the times, now passed through two years,
were turning the stars again toward their eastern courses,
when the leader of the Nile saw these dreams.
For he seemed, while he looks at the pleasant river,
to see seven heifers with sleek bodies,
cropping the growing grass on the green bank;
[and] others, foul with leanness, bring up their steps after them,
and while — wonder! — sluggish, they barely cling to their bones,
they were swallowing the excellent heifers with gaping mouth.
Dreams not discordant are joined, with equal causes;
behold, he sees seven ears from a fruitful seed,
and others, thin and empty of the grain's seed,
— dreadful to tell! — as it were devouring the heavy crops.
Gloomy, he by no means keeps this vision locked in his mind,
but, anxious, ordered all who were skilled to be present,
asking what the meaning of the hidden matters is.
And when the Memphian augur, consulted, was silent,
he who, released from prison some time before, was serving wine,
the young man, speaks out: that he, as Joseph had explained,
had returned to his lost place, and his companion had been killed.
Men are sent in haste, to take the seer quickly,
freed from every charge, out of the foul vault,
and, his unsightly cheeks and the hair grown long in prison
shaving, make him flourish again in his former beauty.
So the upright man, consulted, gives such words in reply,
and teaches that the cows are messengers of years,
and explains the light ears as seven cycles [of years].

For since the dreams are joined in double visions,
God, with the Thunderer joined, commands them to stand certain.
Rather, while the time is here, while you have the care of healing,

with judges appointed, may govern all Egypt from on high
and claim back fifths from every harvest,
so that the abundance first given by the fruitful lands
may hold good through the barren years, when the crops are consumed.

Noble on the lofty platform of Egypt's seer,
whatever the time of fasting could scarcely take in,
holding full granaries, so that when need required their use,
he might bring out the hidden grain to all who asked.
Afterwards, when dire famine, spread over the whole world,
was forcing the frightened to eat whatever could be chewed,
the people cry out, and demand food from the king.
He bids the chief Joseph give grain to the grieving;
obeying the commands, he filled them all, rejoicing.

sends ten young men from his numerous offspring
to procure for themselves with money grain from afar;

lest, being weak, he be unable to bear the hard toil.

bowing, they sought the ground, and greet their brother,
marvelling at him sitting lofty on a high seat.

When he saw them, the prophet, with remembering mind,
rebukes them, and with many words terrifies them in their fear,
saying they had come to spy out what store of crops there was,
or what men held the rich lands under their governance.

is taken, a sure hostage for all as they return.

and the mules are weighed down heavy with immense loads;
and now midway on the road, while one undoes the ties of his sack,
he lets his brothers see the coins he found.
All do the same, and then, the price found,
marvelling, they praise the chief, vying with one another.

their father welcomes them back, and asks for the one.

lamenting grievously that another son was now gone.

forced them again to procure provisions with money,
yet no one had a mind to retrace his steps to Memphis,
unless their father bade the youngest brother go with them.

joining incense and gum with terebinth,
carrying honey among fragrant scents,
and a double price, lest there be some tangled mistake,
because coins had been stored in the closed sacks.
When Joseph saw them in the splendid hall,

what is, what was, what is said soon to come,
urging that the family migrate, and, with the flocks gathered,
he offers the neighbouring hills of the Arabs to them on their coming,
so that, since the land would be dry for an unbroken five years,

and asks Joseph to take in the throng of his dear ones,
and bids him give free grain to his brothers.

and three hundred coins marked by the stamping anvil.

receive two garments of snowy clothing.

he breathes again, hastening to leave his native land.

leading out young men under fatherly rule, five
and seven times ten, as the formula of Genesis provided.

tells slowly with how many years he is endowed,
what his house is, and what the reason for coming to Canopus,

CHAP. L. And to mourning [they] gave seventy days'
lights, while the throng venerates the tomb of the dead man.
Moreover, his sons mourned for seven days
with abundant tears, Joseph making peace
with his brothers, harmless [now], while he set aside old anger.
He himself too, after he had now worn out a hundred years
and ten, measuring the time of his approaching death,
tells his brothers what order of events was to come,
by which they would be able to retrace their steps and leave the Nile,
provided they carry back his laid-up ashes and bones
and convey [them] with them, to be buried in the tombs of the ancients.
Thus at last, after the bright times of a long life,
he departed, and sought God, and left his body.

1421. The Vulgate version reads the last verse of chapter 48 thus: I give you one portion beyond your brothers. What that portion is, the Itala version explains more clearly: I give you Shechem as a special gift above all your brothers; and the Septuagint translators agree with it. Mart. The city Sichima is the same as Shechem. Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine also read Sichimam instead of partem unam.
